analysis.one_liner: Reauthorizes the nation's water pollution law, funding sewage treatment and tightening limits on toxic discharges.
analysis.headline: After nine hearings and a favorable subcommittee vote, the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee ordered a different bill reported in this one's place, and neither received a Senate floor vote before the 103rd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would reauthorize the federal Clean Water Act through fiscal year 2000. It puts more money into state revolving loan funds that pay for sewage treatment plants, lets states forgive loan principal so poorer communities' sewer bills stay below 1.5% of local median household income, and authorizes up to $2.5 billion a year in federal water program funding, with more if deficit targets are met. It also requires EPA to set discharge limits for toxic pollutants, phase out discharges of pollutants that are toxic and build up in living tissue, stop hazardous waste from being piped into municipal sewage plants, and make large dischargers file pollution prevention plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people who swim, fish, and drink from the nation's waters; residents of small towns and poorer communities who would get help affording sewage treatment; tribes; and local governments building water infrastructure.

how_it_helps.text: Lets states forgive loan principal for disadvantaged communities so that average residential sewer charges do not exceed 1.5% of the community's median household income [S2][S3]

Expands what state water pollution revolving funds can pay for, extends their authorization through fiscal year 2000, and authorizes $2.5 billion a year, increasing by up to $2.5 billion more if the budget deficit comes in under target [S2][S3]
Requires EPA to set effluent guidelines and pretreatment standards for toxic pollutants and to prohibit discharges of pollutants that are toxic and highly bioaccumulative [S2][S3]
Makes it unlawful to introduce hazardous waste into publicly owned treatment works, ending a loophole through which industrial waste reached sewage plants not designed for it [S2][S3]

Requires permit applicants to submit pollution prevention plans covering at least 20 pollutants, and directs states to plan and control nonpoint pollution from farms, forestry, and construction, with federal funds withheld from states without approved programs [S2][S3]
Increases the share of funds reserved for Indian tribes and lets state revolving funds assist tribal water projects [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Industrial dischargers, which would face tighter effluent limits, a toxic pollutant phase-out, and new fees covering the cost of writing the regulations; agricultural and forestry sources, which would face enforceable practices in impaired watersheds; and the federal treasury, which funds the grants.
analysis.who_pays_short: Industrial dischargers and the federal treasury

drawbacks.text: The tighter effluent guidelines, toxic pollutant phase-out, and new permit-related fees would impose real compliance costs on manufacturers, and those costs can be passed on in prices [S2][S3]

States would take on new mandates, including statewide antidegradation policies, outstanding national resource water designations, monitoring, and watershed and nonpoint programs, with grant funding withheld if they fail to comply [S2]
The funding increases beyond the base $2.5 billion a year were tied to on-budget deficit estimates staying under pre-set levels, so the added money was not guaranteed [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and environmental gains — cleaner lakes and rivers, less toxic discharge, sewage systems poorer communities can afford — are large and broad. The costs fall on a concentrated set of industrial dischargers and on federal and state budgets; the bill blunts them with fee waivers for small business, loan forgiveness for disadvantaged communities, and a funding trigger tied to deficit targets. The design leans heavily on EPA rulemaking capacity, which was a fair point of concern, but on balance the benefits outweigh the costs for ordinary households.

outcome.mechanism: The bill got months of hearings and a favorable subcommittee vote, but the full committee ended its consideration by ordering a different bill, S.2093, reported in this one's place, and neither bill ever came to the Senate floor before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Max Baucus introduced the bill on June 15, 1993, joined by Senator John Chafee, the committee's senior Republican [S1][S3][S4]
The Senate referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, and its Clean Water, Fisheries subcommittee held nine days of hearings between June and September 1993 [S5]
On February 2, 1994, the subcommittee approved the bill favorably for full committee consideration without amendment [S5]
The full committee met in markup on February 23-25, 1994, and ordered reported an original measure, S.2093, in lieu of this bill [S5]
Neither this bill nor its replacement shows any further action; the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995, without a Senate vote or a clean water reauthorization [S1][S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industrial dischargers — chemical plants, pesticide makers, paper mills, and other facilities that would have faced stricter toxic discharge limits, a phase-out of bioaccumulative pollutants, and new fees — were better off with the bill dead. Local governments and tribes also lost the added water infrastructure money, since no reauthorization passed at all.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Industrial dischargers; municipalities lost funding too

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democratic chairman with the committee's senior Republican as its cosponsor, and the record shows no partisan split in its treatment; it died without a roll call that would reveal one.

industries.industry: Industrial dischargers (chemical, paper, metal, and other point sources)
industries.note: The bill would require stricter technology-based effluent limits, pretreatment standards, a phase-out of toxic and highly bioaccumulative pollutants, pollution prevention plans, and fees covering the cost of writing the rules. Its stricter limits are the mechanism by which the public gets cleaner water, so the industry's interest runs against it.

Registrants would have to supply the data EPA needs to publish water quality criteria for their products unless the product will not reach surface water, and companies filing premanufacture notices under toxic substances law would face a similar requirement.

industries.industry: Municipal wastewater utilities and local governments
industries.note: They gain financing through expanded revolving funds, loan forgiveness for disadvantaged communities, and up to 15-year permits for long-term combined sewer overflow plans, but they also absorb new mandates on stormwater, sewer overflows, and watershed planning.

industries.industry: Water infrastructure construction and engineering firms
industries.note: An authorized $2.5 billion a year in revolving fund capitalization through fiscal year 2000 would flow to sewage treatment and related projects they build and design.

Nonpoint sources in impaired watersheds would face enforceable best management practices, but the bill also makes those areas eligible for water quality incentive payments, conservation programs, and environmental easements.
